Landed living at The Brighton Collection takes on a thoughtful, enduring vision
article:
Intergenerational living has become one of the strongest draws for landed home buyers today, and it is the concept driving The Brighton Collection — a trio of freehold terraced houses in District 19.

Located at 8, 8A and 8B Brighton Crescent, the project by homegrown boutique real estate developer FRX Capital has been named Top Landed Development at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The Brighton Collection comprises two corner terraced homes and one intermediate terraced home within Serangoon Garden, a sought-after landed residential estate known for its tranquillity, strong community appeal, and proximity to the beloved Chomp Chomp Food Centre.

Each unit has two storeys, a basement and an attic, with estimated land sizes ranging from 2,168 to 3,018 sq ft as well as built-up areas of between 5,955 and 7,256 sq ft.

The homes are configured to support multigenerational living, with up to five bedrooms and five en suite bathrooms each.

“Buyers appreciated how the homes maximise every square foot of land without compromising on luxury, comfort or quality. The five-bedroom configuration and generous bedroom sizes were particularly well-received by families who genuinely needed the space,” says a spokesperson for FRX Capital.

“From the high-speed lift to the thoughtfully handpicked fittings, every detail reflects a careful balance between practicality and refined living, creating homes that are functional by design, yet luxurious in experience.”

The developer had acquired the bungalow at 8 Brighton Crescent for $12.4 million last March, before redeveloping it into the three terraced units. FRX Capital launched the trio for sale in October 2025, with asking prices of $6.8 million to $8.3 million.

Tropical modern, by design

DS Architects designed the homes around a tropical modern approach, applying the principle that form follows function, adapted to Singapore’s climate.

Rather than relying on unnecessary complexity, the architecture embraces clarity and purpose, prioritising natural light, ventilation and liveability throughout.

A refined front box frame defines the façade, establishing a strong yet understated presence. Carefully proportioned, the framing element adds structure and definition, avoiding the imposing scale often associated with larger landed homes, while still conveying a sense of modern elegance.

A key feature of the design is the sheltered, generously sized basement carpark. By relocating parking below ground, each home benefits from ample space to comfortably accommodate multiple vehicles.

With the main living spaces elevated above the carpark, the homes enjoy enhanced privacy, improved access to natural light and a more considered spatial hierarchy.

The freed-up ground level further enables seamless integration of lifestyle spaces, with living areas flowing into outdoor decking zones, ideal for family gatherings and entertainment.

In addition, the central courtyard enhances cross-ventilation, keeping the home open and breathable.

Understated and sustainable

Inside, clean lines and a neutral material palette create a calm, timeless backdrop.

“Every home is designed to unlock the full potential of its land, maximising space while creating room for life to unfold. More than architecture, it is a canvas for the owner’s signature — a home that evolves with its residents, gathering character, memories and meaning through the years,” says DS Architects’ director Koh Choon Ngee.

The design of the three Brighton Crescent houses takes a holistic approach to sustainability, integrating architectural strategies, considered material choices and smart-home technologies as part of a more responsible way of living.

This includes the use of recycled and repurposed construction materials, such as building waste incorporated into hardcore layers and certified recycled laminates.

Energy-efficient and smart-enabled systems are also integrated throughout.

The homes are equipped with a premium suite of Fisher & Paykel appliances, incorporating intelligent and safety-driven technologies.

Selected appliances are WiFi-enabled and integrated with the SmartHQ app, allowing residents to monitor, operate and receive notifications remotely.

A visual-audio intercom system, paired with a mobile app, lets residents manage visitor access remotely with greater convenience.

Swift sell-out

In an exclusive early-access event ahead of the official launch, a carefully targeted audience had been introduced to the homes — and their efficient space planning, thoughtful design and concept of multigenerational living.

The campaign appealed to families upgrading from HDB flats and condos, as well as existing landed homeowners seeking a newly rebuilt, more functional and luxurious home without the complexities of reconstruction.

This approach translated into strong early-buyer response, with all three homes sold within months of launch, primarily on the strength of the floor plans and the project’s conceptual positioning.

Going by URA Realis caveat data, the five-bedroom corner terraced house at 8B Brighton Crescent was sold for $7.8 million this January, while the four-bedroom intermediate terraced house at 8A Brighton Crescent was transacted at $6.8 million in April.

The Brighton Collection development is scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027.

title: Bidadari Park: An award-winning urban landscape and biophilic sanctuary
article:
Bidadari Park is a vibrant 13ha destination that serves as the ecological spine of the Bidadari public housing estate.

Designed by CPG Consultants with landscape architecture by Henning Larsen, the public park blends ecological conservation, innovative stormwater management and rich heritage within a high-density residential area.

A joint effort by HDB, National Parks Board and national water agency PUB, the project has been recognised for Excellence in Urban Park Landscape at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The park seamlessly connects surrounding residential neighbourhoods, commercial and lifestyle amenities, as well as transport infrastructure, forming a cohesive and convenient live-work-play environment.

Residents and visitors can access the park via sheltered walkways and connections from MRT and bus interchanges, a 100m elevated land bridge linking residential estates on higher ground, and a dedicated link bridge from The Woodleigh Mall.

Completed in 2024, the park is bounded by Bidadari Park Drive, Bartley Walk, Upper Aljunied Road and Sang Nila Utama Road.

"Bidadari Park is interesting because it’s next to a [former] cemetery, and the existing site has many resident and migratory birds,” says Ng Sze Oun, director of Compound Collaborative and an EPEA 2026 judge in the Landscape Design specialisation.

“They have taken the opportunity to create a habitat that is more focused on nature than on people,” he adds.

Climate resilience and water-sensitive infrastructure

Bidadari Park serves as a blueprint for climate-focused urban planning, incorporating Singapore’s first multifunctional drainage system within a public park.

At its centre lies the 1.8ha Alkaff Lake, a recreational waterbody that also functions as a stormwater retention pond during heavy rain.

It can hold up to 40,000 cubic metres of water — equivalent to 16 Olympic-sized swimming pools — and regulates stormwater discharge downstream to mitigate flood risks for the estate and surrounding areas.

All of the stormwater in the park is managed on-site through a network of naturalised swales, marshes, wetlands and cascading streams — instead of conventional concrete drains.

Rainwater is filtered through dense vegetation and channelled towards Alkaff Lake, while terraced wetlands help remove sediments, nutrients and pollutants from surface runoff.

Gross pollutant traps installed upstream intercept floating debris, litter and pollutants before stormwater enters the lake system.

An integrated public warning and flood management system also provides timely alerts and evacuation notices when rising water levels are anticipated.

Another engineering feature is Singapore’s first underground service reservoir, concealed beneath a community playfield. It stores treated drinking water for the surrounding township while allowing the space above to be used for recreation.

Woodland sanctuary for biodiversity

Guided by core design principles to protect the existing terrain, the development retained approximately 84% of mature trees on-site, including those on the iconic Rain Tree Island situated within Alkaff Lake.

To enrich the local ecosystem, over 170 species of native plants — totalling roughly 140,000 plants — were added across the park, expanding ecological diversity in the vicinity.

Existing woodlands were also carefully preserved and enhanced with dense native planting to create a continuous shaded canopy that improves air quality, reduces urban heat and further strengthens biodiversity within the estate.

Sustainable construction practices were adopted throughout the development.

Felled trees were repurposed into site furniture and habitat logs, and all horticultural waste was recycled.

Rubble stones salvaged from former cemetery structures were reused as paving materials, while demolished concrete aggregates were also reused in woodland trails.

Designated “no-light zones” in ecologically sensitive woodland areas minimise disturbance to nocturnal wildlife and reduce energy consumption.

Today, Bidadari Park represents one of the last two remaining woodland sanctuaries in Singapore for endangered migratory bird species along the East-Australasian Flyway.

The park supports over 193 species of wildlife, including more than 160 species of resident and migratory birds.

Species such as the Changeable Hawk-Eagle, Brahminy Kite, White-Throated Kingfisher and rare Ruddy Kingfisher have returned to the site, which points to improving ecosystem health and freshwater habitat quality.

Meanwhile, Oriental Pied Hornbills have successfully nested and fledged young within the woodlands.

Connecting communities through nature

Designed to foster active living, the park features over 6km of nature trails and boardwalks, alongside a 2km barrier-free greenway connecting surrounding residential precincts to the park.

Sheltered linkways and other transport connections provide all-weather access across the estate, supporting recreational activities such as walking, jogging and cycling.

One of the park’s most distinct features is the 100m land bridge that links higher-ground residential estates, designed as Singapore’s first eco -pedestrian linkway to accommodate both wildlife and pedestrian movements.

In addition, residents can experience a distinct side of Bidadari by walking along the approximately 300m Heritage Walk — created from the former Upper Aljunied Road and featuring interpretive storyboards celebrating the site’s cultural identity — and visiting the memorial garden with conserved relics and naturalistic planting.

The enhancement of existing woodlands has also encouraged the return of birdwatchers and wildlife enthusiasts.

Shared spaces including bird observation pods, nest shelters and viewing decks bring communities together to discover wildlife, exchange knowledge, and participate in ecological learning programmes.

At Adventure Playwoods, children can move freely among logs, plants and play features integrated into the natural landscape beneath mature rain tree canopies.

Lakefront lawns, picnic areas and cafés provide further opportunities for social interaction.

With its integrated landscape infrastructure and ecological features, Bidadari Park brings residents close to nature and biodiversity, community spaces and leisure amenities, enhancing the liveability of the surrounding residential neighbourhoods.

title: STI’s Red October 2026: 4 SGX Blue Chips Still in the Green
article:
October was a rough month for Singapore’s blue chips.
The
SPDR STI ETF
(SGX: ES3), which tracks Singapore’s
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), handed investors a total return of negative 5.5% for the month.
Not every
blue chip
followed it down.
STI’s Green Blue Chips (October 2026)
Company Name & Ticker
October Return
Dividend / Payout Action
DFI Retail
(SGX: D01)
+9.4%
Interim dividend +77% YoY to US$0.062 per share (2027 payout ratio raised to 80%)
Jardine Matheson
(SGX: J36)
+8.2%
Interim dividend +8% YoY to US$0.65 per share (FY guidance: ≥ US$2.47)
Hongkong Land
(SGX: H78)
+3.1%
Interim dividend +33% YoY to US$0.08 per share
Sembcorp Industries
(SGX: U96)
+1.0%
Interim dividend +22% YoY to S$0.11 per share
Source: Fiscal.AI, YoY: year on year.
Here’s the thing: three of the four belong to the same family.
Jardine Matheson counts DFI Retail and Hongkong Land among its key operating units.
And all four have
raised their dividends
or payout commitments this year.
Of course, one month of returns says little on its own.
The business underneath tells you more.
Is DFI Retail’s profit growing faster than its sales?
DFI Retail is a pan-Asian retailer with 7,659 outlets across 12 markets.
For context, DFI put out a business update for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), so it didn’t disclose revenue, net profit or free cash flow.
Underlying subsidiary sales from continuing businesses rose 4% YoY, while underlying subsidiary profit grew 17%.
In other words, DFI is squeezing more profit out of each sale.
Health & Beauty and Home Furnishings became more profitable, and cost cuts lowered expenses.
DFI also swung to net cash of US$128 million as at 30 September 2026, from net debt of US$22 million three months earlier.
Management raised the bottom of its 2026 underlying profit guidance, which now sits at US$295 million to US$305 million.
It confirmed a 70% payout ratio for 2026 and raised it to 80% for 2027.
DFI is also swapping its Maxim’s stake for Maxim’s Starbucks business in seven Asian markets.
The deal should complete by end-March 2027.
Investors will watch how smoothly DFI absorbs it.
Can Jardine Matheson grow profit while revenue falls?
Jardine Matheson is a diversified, Asia-focused investment company.
Its first-half 2026 (1H2026) numbers look odd.
Revenue fell 7% YoY to US$15.9 billion, yet adjusted underlying profit attributable to shareholders rose 9% to US$735 million.
How did Jardine pull that off?
Higher contributions from Hongkong Land, DFI Retail and Jardine Pacific, plus lower financing costs, more than made up for an 8% drop in Astra’s contribution.
One caveat: US$24 million of Jardine Pacific’s gain came from non-recurring items.
Jardine raised its interim dividend by 8% YoY to US$0.65 per share and now guides for at least US$2.47 per share for the full year.
It also launched a US$500 million share buyback.
The cash picture is less rosy.
Free cash flow fell 23% YoY to US$1.5 billion.
As at 30 June 2026, borrowings of US$14.8 billion exceeded cash of US$7.5 billion.
The planned US$2.4 billion purchase of I-MED Radiology Network will also draw on cash.
Is Hongkong Land’s dividend hike backed by cash?
Hongkong Land owns and manages premium mixed-use property in Asian gateway cities.
Its 1H2026 underlying profit attributable to shareholders rose 11% YoY to US$259.1 million.
Underlying earnings per share rose 14% to US$0.1207 on a smaller share count.
Look closer, and operating profit barely moved.
Most of the gain came from lower net financing charges, which fell to US$56.2 million from US$88 million.
Hongkong Land has now recycled US$3.7 billion of capital, or 93% of its target.
The interim dividend rose by a third to US$0.08 per share.
That’s around 66% of underlying earnings per share.
Free cash flow went the other way – it fell 26% YoY to US$153.2 million as spending on major renovations nearly doubled.
Why does Sembcorp make the list despite falling profit?
Sembcorp Industries
is an energy and urban solutions provider backed by Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore.
Its 1H2026 revenue climbed 28% YoY to S$3.8 billion on higher energy prices in Singapore and a month’s contribution from Alinta, its newly acquired Australian business.
Profit told a different story.
Net profit attributable to shareholders fell 72% to S$150 million after S$155 million of Alinta transaction costs.
Underlying net profit fell a milder 25% to S$369 million.
Sembcorp still raised its interim dividend by 22% YoY to S$0.11 per share.
Management expects a stronger second half, with help from a new 600MW hydrogen-ready plant, due for completion in 4Q2026, and a full period of Alinta.
Of the four, Sembcorp has the most to prove.
Free cash flow swung to negative S$39 million from positive S$241 million a year ago.
Borrowings rose to S$15.2 billion from S$9 billion at end-2025.
Get Smart: Follow the cash, not just the dividend
A rising dividend is a good sign, but it isn’t the whole story.
Jardine, Hongkong Land and Sembcorp all raised their dividends while free cash flow fell.
DFI didn’t disclose it.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends.
So when a company you own raises its dividend, check whether cash flow grew alongside it.
If it didn’t, find out whether a one-off spending caused the dip, or whether debt is filling the gap.
One good month won’t tell you that.
The next few sets of results will.

title: Stocks, bonds climb after US election as oil sinks
article:
(Nov 5) : A Democratic sweep of Congress that highlighted opposition of the Iran war extended this week’s plunge in oil prices, helping drive stocks and bonds to big post-election gains.

The S&P 500 rose 1.6%, the most since August. Microsoft Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and Apple Inc. each climbed over 5%. Treasury yields fell across the curve. The dollar had its worst day in two months. Bitcoin topped US$80,000. A nearly 10% tumble in Brent crude sent its price below US$100.

Investors appeared willing to look past the political upheaval, betting the main drivers of US growth, from consumer spending to the artificial-intelligence boom, would remain intact. Political gridlock could curb further fiscal expansion and ease pressure on bonds, offering support for stocks.

“Gridlock is good,” said Jason Pride at Glenmede. “Markets have historically fared better when no single party can push through legislation on party-line votes. This sort of backdrop has generally been supportive for equities.”

While Democratic gains could complicate data-center development in some states, many investors see little immediate threat to the AI investment picture.

Greater congressional oversight will not necessarily derail the AI investment cycle as underlying demand is still solid, according to Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Global Wealth Management.

See also: Asian tech stocks to rise on AI rally amid US votes

“Yes, potential worries over AI regulation are high, but the reality is markets hate uncertainty and now with the election out of the way, we are seeing buyers step in across the board,” said Ryan Detrick at Carson Group.

US stocks are set for gains into year-end as the election removes a source of uncertainty, earnings remain strong and lackluster investor positioning leaves room for renewed buying, noted Citadel Securities’ Scott Rubner.

Since 1946, stocks have been higher one year after every midterm vote, including all four instances when both the House and Senate flipped to the party opposing the president, said Keith Lerner at Truist Advisory Services Inc.

See also: AMD forecast exceeds estimates after AI chip demand soars

“That supports our base case of giving the bull market the benefit of the doubt, but earnings, the economy, interest rates, valuations, and market trends remain more important to our view,” he added.
